reading.title: A school garden that measures its own water
reading.passage:
A. When the science teachers at Hillcrest School started a vegetable garden, they expected the main problem to be pests. Instead, the biggest difficulty was water. In the first summer, some beds were flooded while others dried out, and nobody knew exactly how much water each bed received.

B. In the second year, a group of fifteen-year-old students offered to collect data. They placed a simple rain gauge in the middle of the garden and pushed small moisture sensors into six of the twelve beds. Every afternoon, two students wrote down the readings in a shared notebook. They did not water any bed until they had checked its sensor.

C. After eight weeks, the notebook showed a clear pattern. Beds near the wall stayed damp for longer because the wall shaded them in the afternoon. Beds in the open dried out almost twice as fast. The students also noticed that the old habit of watering every bed at the same time had wasted water on beds that did not need it.

D. The group suggested a new routine. Shaded beds would be watered every third day, and open beds every day during hot weeks. The headteacher agreed to try the routine for the rest of the season. By the end of the summer, the school had used less water than in the first year, although the students pointed out that the summer had also been cooler.

E. The project did not end there. The students wrote a short guide for next year's group, explaining how to read the sensors and why the records mattered. In their final report, they warned that six sensors could not describe every bed perfectly, and they recommended buying more if the budget allowed.

options: Water was not shared evenly between the beds
The students had no time to help
The beds were too close to the wall
questions.key: Water was not shared evenly between the beds
questions.evidence: A: some beds were flooded while others dried out

questions.evidence: B: moisture sensors into six of the twelve beds

questions.evidence: C: Beds near the wall stayed damp for longer ... Beds in the open dried out almost twice as fast

questions.evidence: The passage reports water use, not vegetable size

options: To show that the new routine had failed
To explain that the lower water use may not be due only to the routine
To ask for a larger budget
To prove that the wall gave more shade
questions.key: To explain that the lower water use may not be due only to the routine
questions.evidence: D: less water ... although the students pointed out that the summer had also been cooler

options: How pests were removed from a school garden

questions.key: Students using simple records to improve watering

reading.title: Night buses in a growing city
reading.passage:
A. For many years, the city of Darvan had no public transport after eleven o'clock at night. Hospital workers, cleaners and students who finished late had to walk, pay for taxis, or ask friends for lifts. In 2023, the transport office decided to test two night bus routes for six months.

B. The planners did not simply guess where the buses should go. First, they asked large employers how many staff finished work late. Then they studied taxi records, which showed the most common late journeys. The two routes they chose connected the main hospital, the university and three large housing areas. Buses were planned to run every forty minutes until five in the morning.

C. During the trial, each bus counted passengers automatically as they boarded. On weekdays, the buses carried an average of 40 passengers per journey, but at weekends the figure rose to more than 70. The transport office had expected most passengers to be young people leaving restaurants, so it was surprised that nearly half were travelling to or from work.

D. Not everything went smoothly. Drivers reported that some stops were poorly lit, and several passengers said they felt unsafe while waiting. The office added lights to eight stops in the third month. It also changed one timetable after nurses explained that the bus left the hospital five minutes before their shifts ended.

E. At the end of the trial, the office made both routes permanent and promised to review the timetables every year. A local newspaper called the trial a success, but the transport office was more careful. Its report said that the routes still lost money and that their future would depend on whether passenger numbers continued to grow.

questions.q: Before the trial, there was no public transport after _____ o'clock at night.
questions.evidence: A: no public transport after eleven o'clock at night

options: They used information from employers and taxi records
They asked passengers to vote online
questions.key: They used information from employers and taxi records
questions.evidence: B: asked large employers ... studied taxi records

questions.evidence: C: On weekdays, the buses carried an average of 40 passengers per journey ... at weekends the figure rose to more than 70

questions.evidence: C: it was surprised that nearly half were travelling to or from work

questions.evidence: Ticket prices are not mentioned

questions.evidence: D: The office added lights ... It also changed one timetable

questions.q: What is the transport office's view in paragraph E?
options: The trial was a complete success
The routes have a future only if more people use them
questions.key: The routes have a future only if more people use them
questions.evidence: E: their future would depend on whether passenger numbers continued to grow

reading.title: Why some museums let visitors touch
reading.passage:
A. For most of the last century, museums followed a simple rule: visitors could look, but they could not touch. Objects were kept behind glass, and guards reminded anyone who came too close. The rule protected valuable items, but it also meant that many people experienced museums as quiet, distant places.

B. In recent years, a number of museums have introduced 'handling collections'. These are groups of objects, often copies or less fragile items, that visitors are allowed to pick up and examine. A regional museum in the north of the country, for example, now offers a table of old farming tools, while a science museum lets visitors hold real rock samples.

C. Supporters argue that touch helps people to understand objects in ways that sight alone cannot. Holding a heavy iron tool, they say, makes it easier to imagine the effort of farm work two hundred years ago. Teachers have also reported that pupils who struggle to concentrate on written labels often stay longer at handling tables.

D. However, the change has critics. Some curators worry that handling collections give visitors a false idea of the past, because copies may look and feel different from the originals. Others point out that every object handled will eventually show wear, so museums must spend money replacing or repairing items. A few also argue that the excitement of touching can distract from careful observation.

E. Most museums have tried to balance these concerns. Staff usually supervise handling tables, and labels explain clearly whether an object is an original or a copy. Some museums also ask visitors to describe what they notice before they pick anything up. Whether touch truly improves learning is still being studied, but few museums that have started handling collections have chosen to stop.

questions.q: According to paragraph A, what was one disadvantage of the 'look, don't touch' rule?
options: Museums felt distant to many people
questions.key: Museums felt distant to many people
questions.evidence: A: many people experienced museums as quiet, distant places

questions.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph B?
options: To explain what handling collections are and give examples
To describe the history of farming tools
questions.key: To explain what handling collections are and give examples
questions.evidence: B defines handling collections and gives two examples

questions.q: All objects in handling collections are copies.
questions.evidence: B: often copies or less fragile items ... real rock samples

questions.q: Some teachers say pupils spend more time at handling tables than reading labels.
questions.evidence: C: pupils who struggle to concentrate on written labels often stay longer at handling tables

questions.q: Handling collections have increased the number of museum visitors.
questions.evidence: Visitor numbers are not reported

questions.q: Which of these is NOT given in paragraph D as a criticism?
options: Copies may give a false idea of the past
Objects wear out and cost money to replace
Touching may distract from careful looking
Handling tables take space from original exhibits
questions.key: Handling tables take space from original exhibits
questions.evidence: D lists false idea, wear and cost, and distraction only

questions.q: What does the writer suggest in the final sentence?
options: Research has proved that touch improves learning
Museums are likely to keep handling collections

questions.key: Museums are likely to keep handling collections
questions.evidence: E: few museums that have started handling collections have chosen to stop

reading.title: Learning a language with short daily lessons
reading.passage:
A. Language-learning apps often promise that a few minutes a day is enough to make progress. To test this claim, a university research group followed 120 adult beginners who were learning Spanish for three months. Half of them studied for ten minutes every day; the other half studied for seventy minutes once a week. Both groups therefore spent the same total time learning, and both used the same app and the same lessons.

B. At the end of the three months, the daily group remembered more vocabulary. On a test of 200 common words, they scored on average 15 per cent higher than the weekly group. The researchers believe this happened because short, repeated sessions give the brain more chances to recall words before they are forgotten, a process sometimes called 'spaced practice'.

C. The results for speaking were different. When the learners took part in a short conversation with a teacher, the weekly group performed slightly better. The researchers suggest that longer sessions allowed time for more complex activities, such as role plays, which are difficult to fit into ten minutes.

D. The study had limitations. All the participants were volunteers who were already interested in learning a language, so they may have been more motivated than typical learners. In addition, the researchers could not check whether the participants practised outside the study, for example by watching films in Spanish.

E. The research group does not conclude that one method is better. Instead, it recommends combining the two: short daily reviews to keep vocabulary fresh, and at least one longer weekly session for speaking. It also plans a second study with teenagers, who may respond differently, and a longer study to see whether the vocabulary is still remembered after a year.

questions.q: The study followed _____ adult beginners.
questions.evidence: A: followed 120 adult beginners

questions.q: The daily group spent more time studying in total than the weekly group.
questions.evidence: A: Both groups therefore spent the same total time learning

questions.q: The daily group did better on the vocabulary test.
questions.evidence: B: the daily group remembered more vocabulary ... 15 per cent higher

questions.q: Most participants continued learning Spanish after the study.
questions.evidence: The passage does not report what happened after the study

questions.q: In paragraph B, what does 'spaced practice' mean?
options: Studying in a large, quiet room
Recalling information several times with gaps between
questions.key: Recalling information several times with gaps between
questions.evidence: B: short, repeated sessions give the brain more chances to recall words before they are forgotten

questions.q: Why might the weekly group have done better at speaking?
options: Longer sessions left time for activities like role plays
They were younger than the daily group
questions.key: Longer sessions left time for activities like role plays
questions.evidence: C: longer sessions allowed time for more complex activities, such as role plays

questions.q: Which statement best summarises the researchers' recommendation?
options: Use short daily reviews and a longer weekly speaking session
Adults should not use language apps
questions.key: Use short daily reviews and a longer weekly speaking session
questions.evidence: E: combining the two ...

reading.title: The return of the town market
reading.passage:
A. Twenty years ago, the weekly market in the small town of Elmsford closed. Most residents had started driving to a large supermarket on the edge of town, and the few remaining stallholders could no longer earn enough. For years, the market square was used only as a car park.

B. In 2021, a group of local farmers and craftspeople asked the town council for permission to reopen the market on Saturday mornings. The council was cautious. It agreed to a one-year trial on condition that the organisers paid for their own insurance and cleaned the square afterwards.

C. The first few weeks were difficult. Only nine stalls appeared, and bad weather kept many shoppers at home. The organisers responded by adding covered areas and by inviting a local bakery, which quickly became the market's most popular stall. They also began to advertise each week's stallholders on social media, which, according to their own survey, brought in younger shoppers.

D. By the end of the trial, the market had grown to thirty-two stalls. Shops around the square reported more customers on Saturdays, although two cafés complained that market food stalls were taking their business. The council asked the organisers to limit hot-food stalls to four, a compromise that both sides accepted.

E. Supporters say the market has done more than increase trade. They argue that it has given residents a reason to meet in the centre of the town again. Critics reply that a weekly market cannot replace the shops that closed during the past twenty years. Both points may be true: the market is not a solution to every problem, but it has clearly changed how the square is used.

options: Shoppers went to a supermarket and stallholders could not earn enough
questions.key: Shoppers went to a supermarket and stallholders could not earn enough
questions.evidence: A: residents had started driving to a large supermarket ... could no longer earn enough

questions.q: The council paid for the market's insurance during the trial.
questions.evidence: B: on condition that the organisers paid for their own insurance

questions.q: The bakery became the most popular stall.
questions.evidence: C: a local bakery, which quickly became the market's most popular stall

questions.q: The market made more money than the supermarket on Saturdays.
questions.evidence: No comparison of income with the supermarket is given

questions.evidence: D: grown to thirty-two stalls

options: Allowing no more than four hot-food stalls
Moving the market to the supermarket car park
questions.key: Allowing no more than four hot-food stalls
questions.evidence: D: limit hot-food stalls to four, a compromise that both sides accepted

questions.q: What is the writer's overall position in paragraph E?
options: The market has solved the town's problems
The market has limits but has changed how the square is used
questions.key: The market has limits but has changed how the square is used
questions.evidence: E: the market is not a solution to every problem, but it has clearly changed how the square is used

reading.title: Measuring noise in a hospital ward
reading.passage:
A. Patients often say that the hardest part of a hospital stay is not pain but the lack of sleep. In one regional hospital, nurses decided to find out why. Over four weeks, they placed sound meters in two wards and recorded the noise level every minute, day and night. They also kept a diary of events, such as emergencies and visits, so that they could explain unusual readings.

B. The recordings surprised the staff. The loudest moments were not caused by medical equipment, as many had expected, but by conversations at the nurses' station and by the trolleys used to deliver meals and medicine. Night-time noise was lower than daytime noise, but it often rose suddenly when staff changed shifts at eleven o'clock.

C. The nurses introduced several small changes in one ward while the other ward continued as before. Shift handovers moved from the corridor into a side room, soft wheels were fitted to the trolleys, and lights were dimmed after ten o'clock. Staff also agreed to wear shoes that made less noise on the hard floor.

D. After the changes, average night-time noise in the first ward fell by about a quarter, while noise in the second ward stayed much the same. Patients in the first ward also reported sleeping better in a short questionnaire. The nurses were careful to note, however, that patients in the two wards had different illnesses, which might also have affected their sleep.

E. The hospital has now asked other wards to try the same changes. The nurses who led the project believe that the most important lesson was not any single change, but the act of measuring: once staff could see the noise they were making, they were more willing to change their habits.

questions.q: Why did the nurses start the project?
options: To find out why patients slept badly
To reduce the cost of meals
questions.key: To find out why patients slept badly
questions.evidence: A: the lack of sleep ... nurses decided to find out why

questions.q: Medical equipment caused the loudest noises.
questions.evidence: B: The loudest moments were not caused by medical equipment

questions.q: Noise often rose suddenly when staff changed shifts at _____ o'clock.
questions.evidence: B: when staff changed shifts at eleven o'clock

questions.q: Both wards made the same changes.
questions.evidence: C: in one ward while the other ward continued as before

questions.q: The new trolley wheels were the most effective change.
questions.evidence: The effect of each change separately is not reported

questions.q: Why did the nurses mention that patients had different illnesses?
options: To show that the changes had no effect
To warn that something else might explain the difference in sleep
To explain why the questionnaire was short
questions.key: To warn that something else might explain the difference in sleep
questions.evidence: D: different illnesses, which might also have affected their sleep

questions.q: According to the nurses, what was the most important lesson?
options: Measuring the noise made staff willing to change
questions.key: Measuring the noise made staff willing to change
questions.evidence: E: the most important lesson was ... the act of measuring

writing.title: Homework in primary schools
writing.prompt:
Some people believe that children in primary school should not be given homework. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
constructs: Opinion essay: state and keep a clear position.
